speechtext:
I was not privileged to hear all the speech of the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. White); I have surely missed many pearls and gems. But I heard enough to know the meaning that he tried to impress upon us. He said a moment ago that Quebec had been trying to run the country during the last few years. If he means by that that for a
Mobilization Act-Mr,. Picard

long time Quebec knew how to vote and so helped to bring to power the Liberal government that gave ten years of prosperity under Mackenzie King, he is right, and that when Quebec failed the good cause, we got Bennett and depression, he is right.
The hon. gentleman said that Quebec had tried to run the country. What did Quebec get from the running of the country in the way he means? I did not intend to touch on that matter, yet I am prepared to do so. There is a point I should like to bring to the attention of the house; it concerns French Canada's participation in the war and the extensive criticism thereof in the English language press. Many of my colleagues have refuted those insinuations, but I should like to touch briefly on one aspect of the matter, and that is the apparent success at times of some extremists and demagogues in Quebec who appeal to prejudice in the same way as my hon. friend did a moment ago. These people do not represent Quebec any more than the hon. gentleman represents English-speaking Canada, I hope. They represent a group of extremists who are a small minority, just the same as the hon. member represents a group or caste or school that, happily for Canada, is still a minority in English-speaking Canada.
One of the strongest arguments of those in Quebec who oppose our efforts for unity and harmony is that the majority still refuse to deal on equal terms with us and that we are denied our share of privileges.
The hon. gentleman says that we are running the country. It seems to me we are getting very poor results if we do run it. That would be a good answer to give to some of the extremists in Quebec. I should like to see some evidence of it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Explain the attitude on the plebiscite.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will get his answer all in due course. I say to my English speaking colleagues: if you want us to carry on the fight for unity and understanding, rather than such appeals to prejudice as have been made this afternoon and are sometimes made in Quebec; if we are to struggle for unity and understanding between all citizens of good will in this country, whether English, French, Scotch, Irish, or central European, I say, give us a chance; give us the means by which we can curb the speeches of those who try to do in Quebec what the hon. gentleman did here this afternoon. Above all, show your good will more than merely in words and appeals to loyalty; give us our share of the public appointments. Do not over-
look our people simply because you have not met them. Do not let the appointments to public control boards and supply boards be the fruit of personal association. Mr. X bringing in Mr. A. because they were on the same board of directors or because A was a good customer of his firm, as has been done so often. Look around and recognize that there are people whom you may not have met in business but who have as good training and education as yourselves. Give us our share, and we shall be in a position to silence the nationalists and extremists in Quebec. Do not expect us to be satisfied to have in Quebec federal public servants who cannot speak French, any more than people in Toronto would be content with men who could not speak English.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Why not speak English?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
The matter has been settled when confederation was made and you will not change it to-day. Our majority partners m the confederation are surprised and horrified by the statements of some of our demagogues but a moment of serious thought would reveal they are themselves building these demagogues. Quebec is misrepresented by the statements of some of our extremists, but it is evident that the appeals of these extremists are strengthened not only by appeals like the one we heard a moment ago but by the poor handling of the practical end of the relations between the different races in Canada, by the sad neglect and oftentimes the disgusting prejudice shown against French Canadians by a certain caste of narrow-minded people in other parts of Canada as evidenced by the words of the hon. member who preceded me. They are supplying the material for our extremists to use in arousing bitterness and resentment against English Canada just the same as the hon. gentleman is trying to arouse bitterness among those of his own language against my people. Have you seen hatred and suspicion breeding from satisfaction and content? Try for a change to treat French Canadians on equal terms, not only in your speeches but in your daily acts. Do not discriminate against them in your industries, even in Quebec, or against their entry into the civil service; or, they being there, do not spend your time trying to justify overlooking their due promotion, as I have seen so often in the twelve years during which I stood with Ernest Lapointe in Ottawa. Give us a square deal; let us start a new deal for French Canada, and the preachings of the extremists will fall flat.
If one analyses carefully the speeches made during the plebiscite campaign, of which there

Mobilization Act-Mr. Picard
is a record, he will find that three-quarters of them were based on these grievances, and on the treatment which the French Canadians consider they deserved but did not get.
Would it not be a clever move to try another method with us? Translate your good intentions into practice, and you will take most of the wind away from these demagogues. They thrive on grievances, just as other gentlemen like the one who spoke before me thrive on prejudices just for the pleasure of it and they will fall flat if you remove those grievances. I would not say to my hon .friend that there is a feeling of love for Britain on the part of 100 per cent of the French Canadians, but I will say that all fair-minded French Canadians, which would include more than 90 per cent of them, have respect for Britain, and admiration for the behaviour of the people of Britain in this war. They have a deep attachment to British institutions, and above all they have great devotion for their homeland, Quebec, and their country, Canada. The best use could be made of that feeling by making them proud partners in confederation and in the national business. If they have an equal share in the profits they will be more than ready to accept an equal share of the liabilities. If you ask from them a full realization of their duties, it is up to you to give them full enj oyment of the same privileges you enjoy.
Once more, sir, this house is in the throes of a discussion as to the most efficient method of mustering Canada's man-power for a total effort for victory. We are going through the same procedure, voicing the pros and cons of conscription for overseas service. Is it truly for the good of the country that we should be again airing our advocacy or our opposition in regard to conscription? Does anything justify the continuation of such a discussion as to the proper method to supply the army with men? Has the present system of recruiting failed? Are our camps empty? Are training facilities not being made use of? Are there not in other branches of the service, such as the navy, the air force and other specialized units, definite waiting lists? I can answer in regard to the navy, because I know of a young man who tried to enlist the other day and was told that he might have to wait a month before he could do so. In short, are there any strategic or definite reasons why we should be again arguing this matter? There are none of which I know. We are at it again as the result of political manoeuvres which succeeded in creating a psychic condition among a certain element of the population. If conscription had not been made a political football from
the very start of the war, conditions in the country to-day would be more conducive to a successful war effort than they are tending to be at present, with the campaign that was started and is still going on, stirring up prejudice and resentment between classes and races in this country. Disinterested observers of the future who study the question without bias will, I am sure, cast all responsibility on the shoulders of those who, for purely political reasons, have agitated public opinion throughout Canada in order to impress upon the population the necessity of a conscription measure. The result of their behaviour has been to cause the country tremendous harm: first, by raising doubts in the minds of Canadians as to the scope and extent of their accomplishments; second, by causing such views to be broadcast in the United States, thereby impairing our publicity over there and creating a false impression concerning our war effort; third, by disrupting national unity by arousing suspicion and anger in the minds of Canadians with regard to the attitude of other Canadians of different racial origin. Those who engineered this campaign may feel proud, politically, to have succeeded-temporarily only-in dividing the Liberals on this question of the best means to supply the army with men. If they could survey their actions purely from the point of view of patriotism, they could not but feel ashamed of the result of what they have done.
As for myself, sir, I am against conscription, not as a matter of principle but as a matter of expediency, in the interests of the efficient prosecution of the war and the best results to be obtained in the struggle we are waging against Hitlerism. Since there is nothing just and fair in war, there never has been devised a means perfectly fair and just of summoning men to the defence of their country. Conscription is no exception to that statement. There is nothing just in the fact that the young and the sane and the strong, should sacrifice their liberty, their leisure, their comfort, sometimes their health and, unfortunately, their lives so that others may prosper or at least may not be enslaved. There is nothing fair in that; but even though no system can be perfectly fair, we must have recourse to one of two systems in order to provide the army with the men it needs. One is the voluntary system, under which mem are invited to join the colours to fight the battles of their country. Up to now in most countries this has been found the only possible means of supplying the air force, the navy and highly specialized units such as the parachute troops, the tank corps and more recently the commandos. The other method is the compulsory system,
Mobilization Act-Mr. Picard

under which men are called up by age groups, given a physical check-up and then either discharged or put in the army.
In a country where there exists a strong national sentiment and close national unity, where there is no doubt that the army is fighting not only ultimately but directly for the protection of the country, either by way of defence or of attack, it would appear that a compulsory method, applied without favour and through selective service, might be the least unfair, if there is anything at all fair ini such a thing as the mobilization of men when we do not have mobilization of labour, of resources or of wealth. Unfortunately, sir, Canada is not in such a position. It is forever trying to build up national unity, which has never been completely achieved; and, unfortunately, it has no true Canadian national sentiment, nor will it have as long as French Canadians-and I admit it for my own part -consider their province to be their country, and as long as English Canadians think more of the empire and of Britain than of Canada. Moreover, no wars in which Canada has participated during the past century have been Canada's wars. They have been imperial wars in which we participated because of our imperial ties. National sentiment cannot be created in a country where at least fifty per cent of the people are not of pure British origin, in connection with the fighting of an imperial war or participation in an imperial adventure.
I have already stated in this house and elsewhere that I consider the present war, in the stage it has now reached, as vastly different from any preceding wars, and I have readily admitted the urgency of an unmitigated war effort. But national sentiment, even though it may be stirred when war exists, cannot be especially created when war is on. Therefore a system which might be defended under given circumstances would be inadvisable when all the elements necessary to its success did not exist; and it should be resorted to for service other than hemispheric defence only if the ultimate security of the country demanded it.
A day or so ago the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) mentioned the examples of Russia, France and so on in regard to compulsory service. As a matter of fact, compulsory service more or less originated following the French revolution, in an attempt to bring about a sort of equality of sacrifice of life, if not equality of sacrifice in other directions such as comfort and wealth and so on. As I have said, it can be applied in. a country where national 
unity exists, and it is the only method that could be devised in Russia and elsewhere which would take account of conditions existing there. It never existed in Italy until the war of 1914. We shall see in a short time what pains of childbirth there were when it was brought out in England in 1916, seventeen months after the start of the last war.
What are the circumstances which concern us to-day as to our participation in the war? We have started out with a voluntary system, and it has up to now met with success. In fact we have barely been able at times to equip the men who enlisted. As it goes, the first policy of the government met with the approval of all the citizens, and it was stated to be, first, the adequate protection of the country; second, larger industrial output of materials not only for our own needs, but also to be supplied to Great Britain and our other allies; third, larger agriculture output not only to feed Canadians but mainly to feed Britain, which was in need of food and, fourth, a well-equipped and trained expeditionary force to share in the united nations' effort to curb the enemy abroad.
Canada has up to now splendidly worked toward that end. It has obtained 470,000 men who enlisted voluntarily for service anywhere, and it has an army of 150,000 mobilized under the National Resources Mobilization Act. My only reproach of the Department of National Defence would be that it has not availed itself sufficiently of the National Resources Mobilization Act to create an adequate territorial army. All the time and energy of the department has been spent on the so-called active force, whose very name implies that the territorial or defence army is to be inactive.
There can be no more inappropriate name for the defence army than the term "reserve army". It is a reserve for what?-a reserve that supplies the active, or the so-called active army-as if our army would become active only when they are on the soil of Great Britain, and only when associated with the imperial army? This spirit is evident at every step in the military set-up. A man mobilized for service in Canada was interesting as long as hope had not been abandoned to make him enlist for service overseas. The trouble is that the government's policy was entrusted to men who never believed in it, and who from the very start had other ideas in mind, and who tried to bring them about either through compulsion or through the moulding of public opinion by the Tory press.
I still maintain that there is nothing absurd or ridiculous in the idea I previously expressed in the house that there should be two different types of army in a country like ours, so long

Mobilization Act-Mr. Picard
as it is made up in the way it is, and so long as we have no closer unity than exists among ourselves. There would be a territorial army for Canada, with conscription for Canada under a process of selective service, forcing all men who could serve or who could be spared from industry or agriculture for the defence of Canada. Then there would be a Canadian expeditionary force to take part in the war elsewhere for the defence of civilization, recruited under the voluntary system by the voluntary passage into it of men already in the territorial army, or by the voluntary enlistment of men not yet called in that army under the mobilization act. Both armies to receive the same proper training to make them fit for modern warfare.
That would give us a balanced war effort, without disturbing national unity. There is nothing absurd in it. What is absurd is the present system of putting a man, who is a conscript, in a regiment of volunteers. I will admit that procedure has no sense. On the other hand, if we are mobilizing units for the defence of Canada and recruiting units for an expeditionary force, both trained in the same way, and if we keep in Canada a little more of the machinery and equipment that we send abroad at present you will ensure a better defence of the country while contributing to the fight against the enemy on other shores.
There is a further point I should like to touch upon. I am getting more and more annoyed with the unfair and unjust campaign against Quebec and against French Canadians on the pretext of their opposition to conscription for service overseas. They are trying, like the hon. member who preceded me, to make the people of Canada believe that French Canadians are unworthy citizens, because they do not like conscription. They are trying to make us believe that they are less patriotic Canadians. To read some of the articles published in the Tory press, one would believe that French Canadians are the only ones in the empire who have opposed conscription for service outside Canada. Many of my colleagues have refuted that by citing the examples of Australia, South Africa and Northern Ireland.
Let me go further than that. Let us examine the whole question of the opposition to compulsory service. The objection to conscription is not a French-Canadian invention, nor is it a monopoly of my fellow compatriots. Allow me to quote an opinion on conscription:
My objection to the employment of compulsion for the purpose of recruiting the army under existing conditions has not been based at all upon abstract attachment to a principle. It is based upon an entirely different ground, namely, that the employment of compulsion
under existing conditions would forfeit what I regard to be of supreme and capital importance, that is, the maintenance of the national unity. That again is an abstract objection, but when translated into concrete terms it means this; if you were to apply, I do not speak of any particular method, but any method of coercion or compulsion, without something in the nature, I will not say of universal, but of general consent, you would defeat your own purpose.
Mark those words:
It would not be a practicable or workable method of making good and filling up the gaps left by the defects of the voluntary system. I am speaking my own view-entirely my own view. My proposition, if I were to formulate one, would be this: Not that I rule out compulsion as an impossible expedient, but that compulsion, if resorted to, ought only to be resorted to, and can only from a practical point of view be resorted to-or, in other words, be made a workable expedient for filling up the gap which you have to supply-with something in the nature of general consent.

speechtext: What is the hon. member reading?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Who said this? I shall answer the hon. member for St. Paul's. Was it a French-Canadian member of parliament? Was it a nationalist speaker from Quebec? Was it one of our cabinet ministers? No; the words were uttered by no other than the Prime Minister of Great Britain on November 2, 1915, fifteen months after the start of the great war. Mr. Asquith had said just previously to that-and there is nothing like old books to get new thoughts-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Did he have a change of mind on that?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
If he did, the hon. member will see in a moment.
Here is a further statement by that British Prime Minister:
I will let the house into a cabinet secret- I hope without breaking any obligations of secrecy or any confidence-and that is that there have been differences of opinion amongst the members of the cabinet as to whether what we need, whether, in other words, wThat I call the full exploitation and employment of the recruitable reservoir can or cannot be obtained without resort to some form of compulsion. I will state my own view. In the first place, I have no abstract objection of any sort or kind to compulsion-in time of war. It is a pure question of practical expediency-how are we going to bring the war to a successful conclusion?
I have many more of these quotations, but I shall have to shorten them, because there are some further points I wish to make before resuming my seat.
An hon. member asked1 me if Mr. Asquith changed his mind. It was on January 5, 1916, that the compulsory service bill was introduced into the British House of Commons. Let us
Mobilization Act-Mr, Picard

see what kind of compulsion it was. Let us remember that it was brought into effect only after seventeen months of war. Let us see what reaction its introduction produced on some hon. members in the house at the time. We will see if Mr. Asquith had changed his mind with respect to the compulsory method, when he spoke on January 5, 1916. This is what he said:
There was considerable controversy in the early autumn of last year as to whether we could best do our duty in the war by persevering with our voluntary system, with such improvements as experience had shown to be necessary, or by the introduction, in some form, of general compulsion. There were great divergences of opinion on that subject, even among those who are ordinarily accustomed to think alike, and they penetrated, as I think I have disclosed before, into the cabinet. I believe that these divergences of view on the general question still exist. My own view is well known, and has been publicly expressed. Speaking for myself for the moment, for myself alone-as I have said I do not propose on this larger issue to speak for all my colleagues-I am of opinion that no case has been made out for general compulsion. I, at any rate, would be no party to a measure which had that for its object.
The bill that I am about to ask leave to introduce is one, I think, which can be sincerely supported by those who, either on principle or, as in my c vvn case, on grounds of expediency, are opposed to what is commonly described as conscription.
The right hon. gentleman then went on to give a full explanation of the bill. Note, Mr. Speaker, to what stratagems they had to resort to bring in a conscription bill. It was in effect a conscription bill, but in principle it was not one. Mr. Asquith a little later on said:
The course we are going to ask parliament to adopt is to provide that, if, after due opportunity of inquiry, it is found that there are single men of military age who have no ground whatever for exemption or excuse, they shall be deemed to have done what everyone agrees it is their duty to the state in times like these to do, and be treated as though they had attested or enlisted. . . . The bill applies to all male British subjects who, on the 15th August, 1915, had attained eighteen years and not attained forty-one years of age, and who, at that date were unmarried or widowers without children dependent upon them.
This method of introducing the bill was not followed by a French Canadian, it was not done in the province of Quebec, but in Great Britain, by Mr. Asquith, the Prime Minister, who tried to sugar-coat the bill so that it would be more easily swallowed. It was not conscription, and yet it was conscription. So that in England in 1915 and 1916 there were men like Mr. Asquith who declared themselves opposed to conscription on grounds of expediency, and there were also men like Sir John Simon who regarded conscription as opposed

to the democratic way of life. He resigned his post of home secretary rather than support the bill. He said:
I confess to have regarded the voluntary system as a vital principle of national life.
He said further:
If the bill passes, what are the real chances of general consent? Are the omens favourable? I ask myself with the full sense of the responsibility it involves what is the position to be if and when this bill reaches the statute book. ... I do beg the government and the House of Commons to consider whether the . . . difficulties, some of them existing already in relation to the administration of other acts of parliament, are not likely to be multiplied?
May I remind the house that the gentleman who uttered these words was no less than the Right Hon. Sir John Simon, who had just resigned as home secretary rather than support the bill. And he was not the only one. I could cite many others, but unfortunately I have not the time at my disposal. I shall quote only one more, Right Hon. J. H. Thomas, who said:
I resent to the full the suggestion that has already been made, that those who are likely to oppose this bill are not in favour of winning the war. Not only are they in favour of winning the war, but they genuinely and sincerely believe that the course they adopt is the best course in the interests of winning the war. Therefore, I do not think it will help matters to hurl charges of that kind.
And that applies to the hon. member who spoke ahead of me. Mr. Thomas went on:
I do beg the house to realize, whatever ministers may say, that there is a deep-rooted suspicion in the minds of the workers of this country, that this position has been forced on the government to-day, not with a view of winning the war, and not because of any military value, but because of a certain section of the press.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Now quote Mr. Churchill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I think the house has had enough for the moment. I can quote Mr. Churchill some other day; I have not the time at my disposal now.
From general considerations of the question of conscription and of French Canada's reaction to it I come now to the bill before us and the attitude I intend to take upon it.
My mind and my heart have been torn asunder on the vote to be given on the measure before us, and I am not ashamed to admit it. I have abstained from following any group in a joint consideration of a concerted attitude to be taken. I have worked and studied and listened and consulted', and I shall be alone responsible for my decision.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Picard
My opposition to conscription, as I stated previously, is not so much one of principle as of expediency and what is best for the efficient conduct of the war. I admit that I would have no repulsion to extending conscription to service overseas if I were conscientiously convinced that it was needed in the interests of our own country. As conditions are at the moment I cannot come to that conclusion; I have no such conviction. On the contrary, I think it would hamper our war effort and make it less efficient and it might bring-I hope not-as Sir John Simon said in England, internal disturbances that would cause more harm to the prosecution of a well balanced war effort than the good that might ensue from a more regular flow of men to the army.
But no matter how much opposed I may be to conscription on the ground of expediency, I cannot ignore the fact that the political plots of the Tories in this house and in the press have forced the conscription issue on the Canadian people and have succeeded in making many people in Canada believe that it is now vital to the winning of the war. As a result of this we are faced to-day with a measure which until a few days ago I thought represented a sincere attempt to conciliate opposing views, much in the same spirit as evidenced1 by Mr. Asquith in introducing military bill No. 2 at Westminster in 1916. Bill No. 80 will give the government all the necessary authority to send the men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act anywhere it thinks fit, and should satisfy those who wish the government to have a free hand1. On the other hand, those who oppose conscription for overseas service had reason to be pleased with the assurances of the Prime Minister that such powers would be used only if absolutely necessary, and he thought they were not necessary at the present time.
However, the speeches of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) and of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), who seemed to be competing with each other, have shown a lack of unity in the cabinet which justifies a greater need of caution from those who have to pass on this measure. As long as it could be viewed as a compromise and a conciliatory effort, the measure was no doubt worthy of most benevolent consideration, because it must be recognized that good government in a country ethnically and geographically composed as ours is must of necessity be the fruit of conciliation and understanding rather than of one-sided decisions.
Against the arguments which prompted me to vote for the measure I had to weigh the
most important factor of the expressed will of the people whom I represent on the issue at stake. I need not go over their reasons again, but it is abundantly evident that not only were my constituents against conscription for overseas but they had unmistakably come to the conclusion and made clear by their vote that they were against releasing the Prime Minister from his pledges despite the personal appeals and pleadings I made to change their views.
Is it not a principle of democracy that a representative of the people should as much as possible express the views of those who have elected him as their representative and vote accordingly unless by doing so he endangers their own interests and impairs their own security or that of the country?
The government appeals to-day to the province of Quebec to change an opinion it has nursed since the South African war-nonparticipation in imperial wars of Britain- and it has not prepared public opinion to understand that our share in the present conflict in its fields of battle abroad and especially in Britain is not to support the empire, that it is a contribution to a war for the survival of our own liberties and our own institutions. Public opinion in Quebec has not been prepared by the government's agencies. Let us admit that the propaganda and information services have been most inadequate, to say the least, as far as French Canada is concerned, and that our people have not been enlightened by members of the government themselves. If they had talked of Canadian interests in the war, they might have been able to convince the French Canadians to accept a compulsory measure at this time; but not having contributed to bring that about, I do not think the government can except its supporters from the province of Quebec to go back to our people now and attempt to convince them overnight that conscription for overseas service had become a matter of life or death for Canada. I would be willing to risk myself in such an effort if I had received any help before. But I cannot do it in a week. You cannot all of a sudden, overnight as it were, change the lifelong sentiments of a people.
I could not be convinced, sir, that I would have acted wrongly if I voted against the measure and as my constituents desired; yet I had a feeling that I would best serve the interests of understanding, of unity, and of the bonne entente if I voted for the amendment. At that point of my hesitations I came across a sentence-which perhaps I had better not quote; however, I will go ahead- when perusing Lord Durham's report on the
Mobilization Act*-Mr, Picard

affairs of British North America which set me to thinking anew as to the course I should follow.
Reviewing the constant flare-ups in Lower Canada between the new English settlers and the French Canadians and analysing the source and reasons of their quarrels, Lord Durham referred to the men of good-will who tried to compromise and to reach a livable understanding, and he concluded with these words:
A few of the French, distinguished by moderate and enlarged views, still condemn the narrow national prejudices and ruinous violence of their countrymen, while they equally resist what they consider the violent and unjust pretensions of a "minority"-
And mind you, sir, at the time the minority was not French, but was English, and ruled with the force of arms Canada at that time.
-and endeavour to form a middle party between the two extremes.
Those who affect to form a middle party exercise no influence on the contending extremes and those who side with the English are regarded by their countrymen with aggravated hatred, as renegades from their race; while they obtain but little of the real affection, confidence, or esteem of those whom they have joined.
These grave words, the fruit of a keen observation in 1839, a close survey of our political history will unfortunately show to have been true very often. Unjust as this reaction may be, it has proved to exist in each crisis which we have gone through in this country.
Willing as I am to work to change the viewpoint and to broaden the horizons of my compatriots on some issues where I am not always in agreement with them, is it wise to separate myself at this moment from them? If I had any hesitations left, the statements of the Minister of National Defence would have wiped them out.
I must say, however, that if I expected by my vote to overthrow the Prime Minister, I would not hesitate to vote for the bill, even if I were next day to be blamed by many people, because I would consider it of the utmost importance to ensure his continuance in office in these days, when more than ever is needed at the helm his wise, guiding hand. Under present conditions, although my own inclination is to vote confidence in the Prime Minister in appreciation of this further conciliatory measure, which, I am sure, he has introduced in the hope of maintaining unity and harmony as well as in the hope of keeping the full strength of the country behind the war effort, I cannot but view with alarm the divergence of views in the cabinet on the effect of the present measure, and I will consider it a duty to heed the expressed wishes of my compatriots and vote against the repeal

of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act. But I wish to assure you, sir, using the words of a British statesman, that:
. . . the choice that faces a member who finds himself divided from his chief is a difficult and painful one.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take
pleasure in congratulating the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) for the magnificent speech he has just delivered, and for the many substantiated arguments he set forth to justify the stand of those who oppose the measure recently introduced by the government.
At the general election of March 1940, the Conservative party leader, as well as the head of the Liberal party, all the Quebec representatives and most of the other members of this house, assured the Canadian people that there would be no conscription for service overseas.
Why give this pledge when we had been at war for seven months and certain developments were already indicating that the conflict would become universal? Simply because our politicians remembered the lessons of the past. Conscription in 1917 had been an absolute failure from the practical point of view. It increased by very little the strength of our armed forces and produced on the other hand the most disastrous results. Its enforcement left in the province of Quebec the distinct impression of an attempt at racial domination, and also the conviction that for some, perhaps for a great many of our fellow citizens, empire interests came before those of Canada, the only homeland the French Canadians have. Moreover, it was very costly in bloodshed and useless hardship, and the wounds it caused are not yet completely healed; above all, it sharply divided the Canadian nation.
The anti-conscription policy preached by the Liberal party for the last twenty-five years and endorsed by all parties prior to the 1940 election, was neither new nor unknown in the different Canadian provinces.
No need to delve far back into the past to recall the statement made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe in this very house in March 1939, as well as the statements uttered by these same leaders in September 1939, when war was declared, and those of the hon. Dr. Manion, then Conservative leader.
At the Quebec provincial election in October 1939, the National Union party, then in power, advocated a non-intervention policy. We saw the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe and

Mobilization Act-Mr. Marier
the former Minister of Public Works and Transport (Mr. Cardin) enter the fight to secure Quebec's approval of the federal government's war policy. They promised that Canada's participation in this war would be voluntary and that there would be no conscription for overseas service. On these terms, the province of Quebec pledged her full support to the war effort and promised to contribute her share generously and loyally, side by side with the other provinces in this dominion.
I recall the flattering remarks she then received on every side. There was no newspaper in Canada that did not extol the broadmindedness of our people, their far-seeing patriotism and will to cooperate. And these qualities, may I add, this broadmindedness, this patriotism and will to cooperate for victory, still exist there.
That election of March, 1940, gave the Liberal party the greatest majority ever returned to this house since Confederation, which proves that the policy of voluntary participation commanded the approval of the whole country and, so far, nothing shows that the Canadian people have changed their minds. Of course, there have been various interpretations of the plebiscite vote. Some claim that it expressed, on the part of the majority, the desire to see conscription for overseas service implemented without delay; others considered it as a simple expression of opinion, authorizing the government and parliament to discuss the matter on its merits and take any step that circumstances might require.
When the plebiscite was submitted to the house in February, I supported the measure. Many forecasts on the duration of the war and its limitation to certain European countries, had not become realities. Conditions had often changed since September, 1939. Above all else, the entry of the United States into the struggle could and did considerably alter the situation; it could even have forced us, for example, to direct our war effort into new channels. I believed, as I still do, that in a democracy the people had the right to release us from any promises made to them. For this reason, on the day of the plebiscite, April 27 last, I requested the electors of Jacques Cartier, whom I have the honour of representing in this house, to answer "yes' to the plebiscite question. I took this stand on the strength of statements made by the right hon. Prime Minister in this house and elsewhere. Here is an excerpt from a speech I delivered over the radio on April 21 last:
Mr. King stated in the house, on February 24 last, that conscription for overseas service is not and may never become necessary; the people, he said, over the radio, on April 7, are not called upon to take a stand on conscription by their vote on the plebiscite question; this matter, if it ever becomes the subject of a debate, will be discussed by parliament who will settle it on its merits.
In stating that the question, if it were ever discussed, would be debated on its merits by parliament, I was merely repeating the words of the Prime Minister, in his radio speech of April 7. I quote;
The question of conscription, properly viewed, is a military question. The place to discuss it is in parliament. What the government now seeks for itself and for parliament is freedom to consider and debate and decide this question, like all other questions concerned vvith the war, unrestricted by any pledge and in the light only of the needs of national security.
Further on he added:
The only place it can satisfactorily be decided whether a particular step is necessary or a particular measure needed, is in parliament. In parliament, the government can state its case and provide the information on which a wise decision can alone be made.
Had the vote in my constituency been negative, I would be bound by the will of my electors and I would have little to add to the clear, complete and eloquent statement of the reasons against repeal of section 3 made by the former Minister of Public Works and Transport, and by the other hon. members who are so strongly opposed to the principle of conscription for overseas service as exemplified by Bill No. 80. But in view of the fact that a large majority of my constituents have, on the contrary, given me an affirmative vote and that, in certain quarters, this vote is construed as a vote in favour of conscription, I feel justified in furnishing additional reasons for my stand.
It seems to me that in order to decide whether parliament should agree to the proposed amendment or not, we need only ask ourselves the following questions and answer them logically and sensibly: does the plebiscite vote mean a vote for conscription? Is conscription for overseas service necessary and, if so, should the reasons for that necessity be submitted to the members of this house, so that they may judge them on their merits? Finally, if the measure is not necessary, is it expedient? Or is it liable to produce disastrous consequences?
Mobilization Act-Mr. Marier

I must thank the right hon. Prime Minister for having answered "no" to the first question. He has emphatically stated that the plebiscite vote did not mean conscription. The excerpts from the radio speeches of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) which he quoted in his speech of June 10 agree with what he has stated on various occasions in this house and elsewhere.
An affirmative answer only involved freedom for the government and parliament to discuss the matter of conscription for service overseas, and to judge it on its merits; it did not imply the obligation to enforce it, whether necessary or not.
Moreover, that is the way the voters in my constituency understood it. They had enough confidence in me to leave me free to state whether I was for or against any measure involving conscription for overseas service. But in so doing they laid upon me a new responsibility. And it is because I deeply feel that responsibility that I have a right to know the reasons for the introduction of this measure. Is it really necessary? I followed closely the speech delivered by the Prime Minister on June 10. I have read it many times; in my opinion, it is a very strong plea by the leader of the government against conscription.
I would like to quote the following words which appear at pages 3238 and 3239 of Hansard:
On February 4, the Minister of Finance gave the reasons for believing that the government's war programme for 1942-43 would constitute the utmost effort of which the country is capable. The minister said:
"I believe that the programme which we plan should for the immediate future, the coming year, be a programme which will strain the human and material resources of this country to the limit. I have, therefore, agreed as Minister of Finance, to a war programme for the coming fiscal year which, in my opinion, and in the opinion of my advisers, is the extreme limit of what this country can do, having in mind its human and' material resources."
The new features in the budget speech we heard yesterday will tax more heavily, if possible, the human and material resources of the nation.
The Prime Minister said, as reported at page 3239:
On February 10, the Minister of National Defence stated that the estimated man-power requirements of the army, for service anvwhere, from January 1, 1942, to March 31, 1943. a period of fifteen months, were 90,000 to 100,000 men Of that number over 50,000 had enlisted by the end of May. That is in a period of IMr. Marier. 1
only five months. These figures show clearly that, at the present time, the voluntary system of recruitment is functioning adequately.
And at page 3241:
How could resort to conscription for overseas service add to our war effort? The one way, in which so far as I can see, it might add to our war effort, would be by securing more men for service in the army overseas than can be secured by voluntary means.
If the size of the overseas army was unlimited; if we did not require men urgently for other purposes as well as for the army; there might be a possibility of increasing the total war effort by conscripting men for the overseas army.
And further on the same page:
Clearly there are no grounds for asserting that compulsion is needed at the present time to secure the men required for service in the army overseas. There is nothing to indicate that its application now would add anything to Canada's total contribution to the winning of the war.
Since that date, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) have enlarged, if possible, upon the Prime Minister's words in that connection. The Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) went farther; he asserted that conscription would hamper our war effort.
If conscription for overseas service is not necessary, why is the amendment to the Mobilization Act introduced at this time? What are the facts by which we may judge this measure on its merits? I cannot find them in the Prime Minister's speech. The voluntary system is supplying more men than required and, the taxing of our resources in men and material to the extreme limit will suffice to meet the requirements of the government's programme up to March 31, 1943. Moreover, the Mobilization Act as it stands empowers the government to conscript all able-bodied men in the country for service in Canada and to train them in exactly the same way as they train volunteers.
In the hour of supreme effort and ultimate sacrifice, what is there to prevent the government from seeking the approval of parliament to the amendment they have now introduced and to launch overseas all the armed forces of Canada, should such a sacrifice or such an effort become necessary? Should conscription become necessary to save the country and to win the war, despite the fact that I, in common with my French-Canadian fellow-citizens, loathe conscription, I would vote for such a measure. But, without necessity or reason and1 despite enemy attacks on both our coasts, despite the more urgent peril requiring stronger forces for our own defence and for the protection of those sources of

Mobilization Act-Mr. Marier
supply on which the very life of Great Britain depends, it is being urged that we put on the statute books a measure admittedly unnecessary at the present time, but which may be made use of by some other government tomorrow or by some other leader who might hold an entirely different view of the situation.
The present Prime Minister has more than any other and throughout his entire career, advocated the supremacy of parliament. I understand the government should hold greater powers in time of war, but when the very lives of our youth, the cream of the nation, are at stake, the members of this house would indeed make a serious mistake and fail in their duty should they renounce the right to decide when and how, in what circumstances and in the face of what danger, the government may take upon themselves the right of disposing of the lives of others. In support of his attitude, the Prime Minister tells us that parliament, by virtue of the Mobilization Act, has already conferred upon the government the power of conscripting men and that the present amendment is but an extension of this power. He overlooks the fact that when they brought down this measure in 1940, the government gave excellent reasons to justify its adoption and that, besides, it was accompanied by another solemn pledge given by the Prime Minister, which can be found on page 854 of Hansard for June 18, 1940:
Once again, I wish to repeat my undertaking, frequently given, that no measure for the conscription of men for overseas service will be introduced by the present administration.
It was on the same day that the Prime Minister announced the armistice parleys between France on the one hand and Italy and Germany on the other. It was in those dark hours when England, together with her dominions and colonies, faced the dark future alone, at an infinitely graver hour than the present one.
Russia was then bound to Germany by a non-aggression pact; we were even anxiously wondering whether she would join our enemies. Japan was as threatening as ever and no one doubted that she would enter the conflict sooner or later.
The United States were still out of the war, and while supplying the allies with credit, arms and munitions, were not extending to them the tremendous support given at the moment.
If the Prime Minister, notwithstanding all this and in spite of the anticipation of an increasing danger, repeated the assurance that
there would be no conscription for overseas service, he undoubtedly did so to maintain in this country the sacred unity which must remain the basis of our war effort.
Is it more expedient to-day than at that time to break our pledges, to stir up popular feeling, to plant the seeds of hatred which extremists have endeavoured to sow throughout the country?
Already an important section of the Canadian people is looked upon with distrust because it voted "no" in the plebiscite. Already, the small group of politicians and financiers who have sworn to overthrow the government and to form a so-called national union government are jeering at Quebec through their hired press and their paid advertisements published on a lavish scale all over Canada and even in the United States.
They play upon the inborn feeling of attachment for Great Britain existing among our English-speaking fellow citizens, just as they make able use of the undeserved reproach that Quebec is not bearing her share of sacrifice for the purpose of winning the war. If Canadian unity is destroyed, if good: understanding between the two main racial groups in the country exists no longer, whose fault is it? The French-Canadian minority has made concession after concession in order to maintain it, as the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres so ably explained.
Is it that unity and good understanding can only be maintained through repeated and constant sacrifices on the part of the minority, in the absence of any reciprocity? Does unity demand that the French Canadians should give up one of the most sacred rights for which we are now fighting, namely, that of freely expressing their opinions? The overwhelming majority of French Canadians have refused to release the government from its commitments or pledges. Had they not a right to do so, since the question of the plebiscite was an open one? The government was released from its past commitments by a large majority. Well and good, we submit to this verdict. But when the government ask that section 3 be repealed, that the principle of conscription be written into the statute books, have we not the right to know the reasons for this attitude and the circumstances which justify it? Is this incompatible with our position as loyal Canadian subjects. The isolation of the province of Quebec has been mentioned. The vote given in the 1940 election is still too recent for us to believe that the overwhelming majority of the people in this country ardently wish for conscription for overseas service and I share the opinion of the Minister of Agriculture when he states that no
Mobilization Act-Mr. Marier

party with a background and a hope for the future could well enforce such a measure. Which shows that, in his opinion, a majority of the electorate is still opposed to conscription for overseas service.
The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) has made an eloquent appeal in favour of trusting the present government. His speech is remarkable by the elevation of thought and by the expression of certain truths good to hear now and again, in this house and through the country as a whole. But the hon. Minister of Justice, who is also a great lawyer, endeavoured to justify the blind vote of confidence the government is asking from the hon. members by quoting the fact that in his profession he always insists that his clients do not interfere in the conduct of a case. I practised that same profession for nearly thirty years and always I demanded the same degree of trust from my clients. But the latter know nothing about the law and they come to us for advice, not to guide us. Thus the minister's argument implies, to my mind, that we have nothing to say in the conduct of the war and that we must invest the government with dictatorial powers. I am sorry to say that the conception I have of a member's responsibility is quite different.
The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, in the course of the remarkable speech he delivered in this house on June 11, stated that one of the reasons of the disunity we deplore to-day lies in the fact that never during the last twenty-five years did Canada have a policy of her own, as becomes a sovereign nation.
This is partly true. We have lived for a long time within the orbit of a great power and we have suffered the repercussions of a policy over which we had little or no control. However, during the last few years and under the guidance of the Prime Minister, who is to be congratulated on this account, our political, financial and economic life has followed pretty closely the pattern set by our country's geographical position. Canada is an American country and if this is taken into account and our policies hence given a purely Canadian trend, many difficulties will be overcome, many causes of disunity will disappear for the greater good of the country. We shall hear less of the two principal nationalities that share our territory and more of the Canadian nation.
I have the highest esteem and regard for the leader of the government, our leader, but I cannot support the proposed amendment to

the Mobilization Act, which implies a change of policy and incorporates in our statute books the principle of conscription for overseas service. Neither can I admit that the government, by a simple order in council, be empowered, under section 5 of the Mobilization Act, to apply conscription without consulting parliament and send overseas thousands of young men drafted hereto for the defence of Canada, and of Canada only.
Moreover, the statements of the Prime Minister and the principal members of his cabinet imply that conscription for overseas service is not necessary, that it might even hamper our war effort. For these various reasons, I feel compelled to vote against this measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
The question which arises to-day in the House of Commons is whether we should give the present government or its successors the power to impose by order in council a measure of conscription for overseas service. Therefore the principle of conscription for military service overseas is at stake in this bill, and it is the Liberal government that presents the bill and asks Liberal members from the province of Quebec to vote to give the government a free hand to put conscription into effect by and by if needed. Speaking for my constituency and for myself, I regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that I will not support the government on this question, that I will vote against it. I am breaking a fifty-three year old tradition when I set myself against the Liberal party in this chamber, and words could not express my regret. As a matter of fact it was in 1889 that Sir Franqois Lemieux was elected Liberal member for the county of Bonaventure, which constituency he wrested from such famous Conservatives as Tarte, Robitaille and Riopel, by whom it had been held since confederation. Since that time, fifty-three years ago, my county has been Liberal, without a single defeat; and I do not think any member from that constituency, including Sir Franqois Lemieux, Hon. Charles Marcil or Hon. Pierre Emile Cote, has ever had to vote against the government and the head of the Liberal party. In a recent radio talk I said about the Hon. Mr. King:
No other prime minister of Canada has so loved the province of Quebec and has treated it with such a measure of justice. I know of no other man who, because of his dignity and honesty, of his exemplary life devoted entirely to his country's service, deserves so much esteem as the Prime Minister.
I cannot understand, however, how it is that the Liberal government, which has always been supported by the province of Quebec, which

Mobilization Act-Mr. Poirier
has represented during many years the true Canadian sentiment not only in Quebec but in a great majority of the constituencies of this country, should now allow itself to be advised by the worst enemies of the Liberal party and of Freneh-Canadian sentiment, and should go from one concession to another even to the point of bringing into parliament a bill containing the principle of conscription for overseas service. It is easy to see that it is high finance that is influencing the will of the government and forcing it to present such a bill. It is high time we offered some resistance to the will of high finance. I say that immediately after the war the people will revolt, peacefully or with violence, against the rapacity of high finance. In my countv of Bonaventure, as in almost every part of the country, people suffered much during the depression of 1930-35. They were told that there was no money to buy bread, and large families were expected to live on relief allowances of S10 to $20 a month. But just as soon as war was declared billions of dollars were found with which to organize it. It is time to realize the financial tyranny which crushes the people of Canada. We are 100 per cent behind the war effort, but on the sole condition that the rapacious financiers be brought to reason, that after the war the riches of the country be put to the service of the people and not the people to the service of the riches.
I wish all my colleagues to understand me, Mr. Speaker. I am a Canadian, and no one loves his country more than I do. My maternal ancestor, a public notary, Alexandre Bourque, came to this country, to Port Royal in Acadia, in 1635; my paternal ancestor came to live in Prince Edward Island shortly after that. Therefore it is more than three hundred years since my forefathers settled in Canada. I represent a county which is representative of the whole of Canada through its components of Acadians, French Canadians and English Canadians. The latter, Scotch, English and Irish, form about 18 per cent of the population. We walk hand in hand, and there are no racial problems in my county. Bonaventure county can be proud of its war effort up to the present. It has furnished to the three Canadian services more than two thousand volunteers, out of a population of 42,000. The families of my county were among the first to be stricken, and more than two hundred of them weep over their sons who have fallen or who are prisoners of war at Hong Kong. The airmen of my county perished gloriously, one after the other, in the near east, in Great Britain, or in the neighbouring zones. Let me
in passing offer to these stricken families the grateful salute of their proud country, which will never die.
We are ready to suffer all sacrifice in order to win this war. We have nobly consented to the general mobilization and to conscription for the defence of Canadian territory. We have consented to the gift of a billion dollars to England. We even would have consented to conscription which would have allowed men to be sent to any part of the American continent, in order to liberate all Canadian volunteers now on Canadian soil. Nevertheless we are not ready to go as far as conscription for overseas, first because we fear that conscription for overseas will disorganize completely the defence of our own country. In my county, Mr. Speaker, there are 120 miles of coastal territory without any military defence whatsoever. We, who have given more volunteers than almost any other part of Canada in proportion to our population, are left exposed to danger at the very door of the gulf of St. Lawrence, without defence of any kind. We have sacrificed the flower of our youth in this present war, with joy, with enthusiasm, with patriotism; but do you think we have been given any credit for it? Not a cent has been spent in my county, and we are supposed to accept this principle of sending the rest of our young men overseas by order in council. The Prime Minister and all the members of his cabinet are in accord that conscription is not necessary, that it perhaps never will be necessary; nevertheless we are asked to vote the principle of conscription. Such an attitude is contradictory.
Why have conscription, Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) declares in this house that there are no more bachelors or widowers without children in two districts, Quebec and Vancouver? Why have conscription when the director of selective service, Mr. Little, officially declares that we are threatened with a very serious shortage of labour, when we are in need of four thousand men in the Arvida war industry in the province of Quebec, and when Ontario war industries could employ twelve thousand more men? Why have conscription when Canadian agriculture lacks farmers and when the fishermen of Gaspe, as well as those of the east, are not numerous enough to fill their contracts with England and furnish the quantity of fish required by the armies of the allies? I would suggest rather that a reasonable and intelligently managed campaign of voluntary enlistment be carried on in those districts where there are still able-bodied men. For example, eveiyone knows that the Gaspe peninsula with a population of eighty thousand

Mobilization Act-Mr. Poirier
has furnished more than four thousand volunteers. We also know that the population of the Gaspe peninsula is spread over a coastal territory of three hundred miles along the St. Lawrence. We know that this population is one of able seamanship, and that its sons would have cut a worthy figure in the Canadian navy. It is hardly believable, but no enlistment office for the navy has ever been opened in that region, and our boys have been forced, under those circumstances, to enlist in the land forces.
I do not want to be unjust toward anyone, and I am glad to admit that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has greatly improved the situation of French Canadians in the Canadian army. He has created new French Canadian regiments. Lately he did all he could to increase the number of French Canadian officers in the army. He has even opened special schools to allow educated French Canadians to follow training courses for officers at St. Jerome, Quebec, and at Brockville, Ontario. I congratulate him. We appreciate his efforts, and we are grateful for all he has done in this direction.
Following the same trend of ideas, I am pleased to recognize publicly in the parliament of my country the tolerance and moderation of the great majority of my English-speaking colleagues. A son of Acadia, I myself belong to a race whose wisdom, calm and moderation have been its strength in the past. Submitted to the greatest trials a people can endure, we have survived, I am glad and proud to say, thanks to the indomitable courage, unending patience and unexampled strength of will of our race. Thanks to these qualities we have succeeded at last in obtaining recognition of a part of our rights. We are ready to walk hand in hand with Canadians of other nationalities. It is with these dispositions that I came here two years ago, and I am happy to say that I have found here English-speaking colleagues who have an open mind and a tolerant soul. They are all filled, as we are, with love for our country. They are ready, I believe with all my heart, to understand the mentality and the aspirations of French Canadians and Acadians. I therefore beg them to make an effort to understand our point of view.
It is clear that in 1940 the honour and the given word of the Canadian people in its entirety were at stake in this promise that there would be no conscription for overseas. The province of Quebec, to whom the repre-

sentatives of the Liberal party had long since promised that we would never participate in the wars of the empire, nevertheless consented to everything, provided there would be no conscription for overseas. Consequently this pledge of honour cannot be broken without the consent of Quebec. Let us therefore continue our voluntary war effort. Let the Minister of National Defence continue to grant his favours and place his confidence in the province of Quebec, and he will see that the volunteers will continue to come into the Canadian forces in ever-growing numbers.
It was Reverend George A. Little of Toronto who said lately before a religious meeting held in Winnipeg that Quebec would surprise the rest of the country by the number of its enlistments, if we went about the matter in the right way. I thank this distinguished clergyman of the Protestant faith for his wide understanding of the French-Canadian point of view. He is right. In spite of the mistakes that have been made in Quebec; in spite of the fact that a free field has been left to anti-British propaganda for two years and a half, the bulk of the French-Canadian population is ready to suffer voluntarily all the sacrifices expected of it.
A great many English-speaking members have expressed the same opinions in the house, and I thank them with all my heart. Many are making an effort to-day to keep intact the bridges which connect the two races. They are right, Mr. Speaker.
Within the last few days the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford) and the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) have tried to create a little harmony between the two races and many others are working in this direction.
The whole of the country will be grateful to them. Let us admit, with the French journal L'Action Catholique, that there are a great many points on which we fully agree; and let us leave aside the only point on which we cannot think alike.
I express the hope, in concluding this speech, that the present crisis will pass, that we will win the war with volunteers without the application of conscription, and that the two great races of Canada will continue together in friendship toward their glorious destiny.
